svg.aria-label: Diagram: how the EventBridge relaunch moves the unit of decomposition from the bus to the subscriber. On the left, Custom Event Bus Classic: the bus owner writes rules and targets, so routing is owned centrally. Its quotas allow up to 100 event buses per account per Region, 300 rules per bus in most Regions, and a fixed maximum of 5 targets per rule, with PutEvents throttled at 10,000 per second in North Virginia, Oregon and Ireland but only 400 per second in most other Regions. Teams that wanted independent routing asked for another bus, which is why the allowance was large. On the right, the new Custom Event Bus: consumers create their own subscriber resources, each filtering events and delivering to over 250 AWS services, so routing is owned by the consumer rather than the bus owner. Its quotas allow only 5 buses owned per account by default, though this is adjustable and buses shared with the account do not count, alongside 10,000 subscribers per bus counting every account the bus is shared with, and 500,000 events per second per bus, which is not adjustable. Retention is 24 hours by default and configurable from 1 to 365 days, retry attempts range from 0 to 185 with a default of 5, event age ranges from 60 to 86,400 seconds with a default of 300, and the deduplication window is fixed at 300 seconds. A central panel records the arithmetic: twenty times fewer buses and fifty times the per-second event ceiling, because the bus became a shared pipe rather than a boundary. A closing panel records the operational catch, that only one subscriber create or delete may be in progress on a bus at a time across every account it is shared with, with a second call failing with ConcurrentModificationException, and that filter changes are capped at 24 per subscriber in any rolling 24 hours.
svg.title: The bus stopped being the boundary; the subscriber became it
svg.text: The headline is a feature list. The quota page says the architecture changed.
You may own 5 buses now, not 100 — because a bus is no longer how teams stay out of each other's way.
Custom Event Bus — Classic
the bus owner writes the rules and targets
routing owned centrally — a consumer must ask
100 event buses per account
300 rules per bus (most Regions)
5 targets per rule — not adjustable
PutEvents 10,000/sec in IAD, PDX, DUB
400/sec in most other Regions
Want independent routing? Ask for another bus.
Custom Event Bus — new
consumers create their own subscribers
routing owned by the consumer — no request needed
5 buses owned per account (adjustable)
10,000 subscribers per bus, across all accounts
500,000 events/sec per bus — not adjustable
retention 24 h default, 1 to 365 days
retries 0–185 (default 5) · age 60–86,400 s
delivers to over 250 AWS services.
The trade, in two numbers
100 ÷ 5 = twenty times fewer buses · 500,000 ÷ 10,000 = fifty times the per-second ceiling
The bus became a shared pipe rather than a fence. Fewer of them, each far larger.
The operational catch the model creates
“Subscriber creates or deletes in progress on one bus: 1 across all accounts; a second call fails with
ConcurrentModificationException.”
Many teams are invited onto one shared bus, then permitted one subscriber mutation at a time between them.
Two pipelines deploying at once, in different accounts, and one fails on a resource neither team owns.
Filter changes: 24 per subscriber in any rolling 24 hours, not configurable — reapplying filters on every deploy will throttle.
Deduplication window fixed at 300 seconds, so consumer idempotency still matters beyond five minutes.
Pricing now charges for data transferred, not events — payload size became the cost lever. Fourteen Regions at launch.
